plain_english: Living up to your nature as a human being isn't easy. But what is a human being? A thinking, mortal creature. What separates us from wild animals? Our ability to reason. What separates us from sheep and other livestock? The same thing. So don't act like a wild animal. If you do, you've stopped being human. You've broken your promise. Don't act like sheep either. If you do, you've also lost what makes you human. How do we act like sheep? When we're greedy, lustful, reckless, dirty, and thoughtless. We've sunk to the level of livestock. What have we lost? Our ability to think. How do we act like wild beasts? When we're hostile, harmful, emotional, and violent. We've dropped down to their level. Some of us become big, dangerous beasts. Others become small, nasty ones. At that point, you might as well say "let a lion eat me." Either way, you've destroyed what it means to be human.
original_excerpt: It is no common (easy) thing to do this only, to fulfil the promise of a man's nature. For what is a man? The answer is, A rational and mortal being. Then by the rational faculty from whom are we separated? From wild beasts. And from what others? From sheep and like animals. Take care then to do nothing like a wild beast; but if you do, you have lost the character of a man; you have not fulfilled your promise. See that you do nothing like a sheep; but if you do, in this case also the man is lost. What then do we do as sheep? When we act gluttonously, when we act lewdly, when we act rashly, filthily, inconsiderately, to what have we declined? To sheep. What have we lost? The rational faculty. When we act contentiously and harmfully and passionately and violently, to what have we declined? To wild beasts. Consequently some of us are great wild beasts, and others little beasts, of a bad disposition and small, whence we may say, Let me be eaten by a lion. But in all these ways the promise of a man acting as a man is destroyed.
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english: When does a complex logical statement work? When it delivers what it promises. A complex statement holds up when all its parts are true. When does an either/or statement work? When it delivers what it promises. When do flutes, lyres, horses, and dogs stay in good condition? When they do what they're supposed to do. So why be surprised that people work the same way? Everyone gets better and stays strong by doing the right actions. Carpenters get better by doing carpentry. Grammar teachers get better by teaching grammar. But if someone gets used to writing with bad grammar, their skill will definitely get worse and fall apart. Modest actions keep a modest person modest. Immodest actions destroy them. Faithful actions keep a faithful person faithful. The opposite actions destroy them. And the flip side also works: opposite actions make opposite traits stronger. Shameless acts make a shameless person more shameless. Unfaithful acts make an unfaithful person more unfaithful. Harsh words make a harsh person harsher. Anger makes an angry person angrier. Taking more than you give makes a greedy person greedier.
original_excerpt: For when is a conjunctive (complex) proposition maintained? When it fulfils what its nature promises; so that the preservation of a complex proposition is when it is a conjunction of truths. When is a disjunctive maintained? When it fulfils what it promises. When are flutes, a lyre, a horse, a dog, preserved? (When they severally keep their promise.) What is the wonder then if man also in like manner is preserved, and in like manner is lost? Each man is improved and preserved by corresponding acts, the carpenter by acts of carpentry, the grammarian by acts of grammar. But if a man accustoms himself to write ungrammatically, of necessity his art will be corrupted and destroyed. Thus modest actions preserve the modest man, and immodest actions destroy him; and actions of fidelity preserve the faithful man, and the contrary actions destroy him. And on the other hand contrary actions strengthen contrary characters: shamelessness strengthens the shameless man, faithlessness the faithless man, abusive words the abusive man, anger the man of an angry temper, and unequal receiving and giving make the avaricious man more avaricious.
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english:
This is why philosophers tell us not to stop at just learning. You need to study, then practice. We've been doing the wrong things for so long. We act on opinions that go against what's true. If we don't practice the right opinions too, we'll just be people who repeat other people's ideas.

Right now, any of us can talk about good and bad things using all the right terms. We say some things are good, some are bad, some don't matter. The good things are virtues and whatever involves virtues. The bad things are the opposite. The things that don't matter are wealth, health, reputation.

But then what happens? If there's a loud noise while we're talking, or someone laughs at us, we get upset. Where's your philosophy now? Where did all those ideas you were just talking about come from? Just your lips. That's all.

Why are you ruining the help others have given you? Why are you treating the most important things like a game of dice?

Storing bread and wine is one thing. Eating them is another. What you eat gets digested and spread through your body. It becomes muscle, flesh, bones, blood. It gives you good color and healthy breath. What you just store away — you can take it out and show it off whenever you want. But that's all you get from it. You just look like you have it.
original_excerpt: For this reason philosophers admonish us not to be satisfied with learning only, but also to add study, and then practice. For we have long been accustomed to do contrary things, and we put in practice opinions which are contrary to true opinions. If then we shall not also put in practice right opinions, we shall be nothing more than the expositors of the opinions of others. For now who among us is not able to discourse according to the rules of art about good and evil things (in this fashion)? That of things some are good, and some are bad, and some are indifferent: the good then are virtues, and the things which participate in virtues; and the bad are the contrary; and the indifferent are wealth, health, reputation. Then, if in the midst of our talk there should happen some greater noise than usual, or some of those who are present should laugh at us, we are disturbed. Philosopher, where are the things which you were talking about? Whence did you produce and utter them? From the lips, and thence only. Why then do you corrupt the aids provided by others? Why do you treat the weightiest matters as if you were playing a game of dice? For it is one thing to lay up bread and wine as in a storehouse, and another thing to eat. That which has been eaten, is digested, distributed, and is become sinews, flesh, bones, blood, healthy color, healthy breath. Whatever is stored up, when you choose you can readily take and show it; but you have no other advantage from it except so far as to appear to possess it.
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher

plain_english: What's the difference between explaining these teachings and explaining the ideas of people who disagree with us? Go ahead — sit down and explain Epicurus's views using proper reasoning. You might even explain his ideas better than Epicurus did himself. So why do you call yourself a Stoic? Why lie to everyone? Why pretend to be Jewish when you're really Greek? Don't you see how people get labeled as Jewish, Syrian, or Egyptian? When we see someone wavering between two sides, we usually say, "This person isn't really Jewish — they're just acting like one." But when someone truly takes on the feelings and adopts the beliefs of Jewish doctrine, then they actually are Jewish, both in fact and in name.
original_excerpt: For what is the difference between explaining these doctrines and those of men who have different opinions? Sit down now and explain according to the rules of art the opinions of Epicurus, and perhaps you will explain his opinions in a more useful manner than Epicurus himself. Why then do you call yourself a Stoic? Why do you deceive the many? Why do you act the part of a Jew, when you are a Greek? Do you not see how (why) each is called a Jew, or a Syrian, or an Egyptian? and when we see a man inclining to two sides, we are accustomed to say, This man is not a Jew, but he acts as one. But when he has assumed the affects of one who has been imbued with Jewish doctrine and has adopted that sect, then he is in fact and he is named a Jew.
source_reference: Discourses, That When We Cannot Fulfil That Which the Character of a Man Promises, We Assume the Character of a Philosopher
